questions.q: What is a spandrel beam?
o: A beam buried only in soil
A beam running along the exterior edge of a floor or roof
questions.ref: Francis D.K. Ching, Building Construction Illustrated - structural systems, retaining walls, frames and slabs
questions.n: Spandrel beams occur at the perimeter of floors and roofs and often support exterior walls or facade systems.

questions.q: Why is a simple shear connection generally insufficient as the only connection at the fixed end of a cantilever?
o: It is used only in concrete
It does not provide the rotational restraint needed to develop the cantilever end moment
questions.ref: AISC Steel Construction Manual - beams, columns, moment connections and structural stability
questions.n: Cantilever action requires rotational fixity and moment transfer at the support.

questions.q: What is a mezzanine?
o: An intermediate partial floor between main stories
questions.ref: Cyril M. Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction - structural terminology
questions.n: A mezzanine is an intermediate or partial floor inserted between principal stories.

questions.q: What structural system consists of thin, deep plates rigidly joined along their longitudinal edges at angles?
questions.ref: Daniel L. Schodek et al., Structures - structural systems, space frames, folded plates and diaphragms
questions.n: Folded-plate structures use connected planar elements whose folds provide stiffness and allow shell-like load transfer.

questions.q: What does structural conceptualization primarily involve?
o: Selecting and arranging structural systems and elements to satisfy function, safety, constructability, and architectural intent
questions.ref: Daniel L. Schodek et al., Structures - structural systems, space frames, folded plates and diaphragms
questions.n: Structural conceptualization is the early-stage development of the structural system, including type, layout, load path, and proportions.

questions.q: What is the horizontal displacement of a building or story under lateral loading called?
questions.ref: ASCE/SEI 7 - Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and Other Structures
questions.n: Structural drift is lateral displacement under loads such as wind or earthquake effects.

questions.q: An architect compares a braced frame, a moment frame, and a shear-wall system for a tall building. What design activity is this?
questions.ref: Daniel L. Schodek et al., Structures - structural systems, space frames, folded plates and diaphragms
questions.n: Evaluating alternative structural systems at an early stage is a core part of structural conceptualization.

questions.q: A wind-loaded frame shows 35 mm horizontal displacement at the fifth floor and 22 mm at the fourth floor. What is the interstory drift between those levels?
questions.ref: ASCE/SEI 7 - Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and Other Structures
questions.n: Interstory drift is the relative displacement between adjacent levels: 35−22=13 mm.

questions.q: Which quantity is most directly associated with torsional loading?
questions.ref: Cyril M. Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction - structural terminology
questions.n: Torque is the moment that produces twisting about an axis.

questions.q: Which building element commonly acts as a diaphragm?
questions.ref: Francis D.K. Ching, Building Construction Illustrated - structural systems, retaining walls, frames and slabs
questions.n: Floor and roof decks or sheathing can act as diaphragms when properly connected and designed for in-plane forces.

questions.q: What failure mode occurs when a retaining wall rotates about its toe because of lateral earth pressure?
questions.ref: NCMA/CMHA and geotechnical retaining-wall guidance - sliding and overturning stability
questions.n: Overturning is rotational instability caused when the overturning moment from lateral pressure exceeds resisting moments.

questions.q: Wind load reaches a building's exterior wall, then is carried through the roof deck to braced frames. What structural action is the roof deck performing?
questions.ref: ASCE/SEI 7 - Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and Other Structures
questions.n: The roof plane is transferring lateral load in its own plane to the vertical lateral-force-resisting system.

questions.q: The top of a retaining wall moves outward while the base remains approximately fixed. Which instability is most consistent with this behavior?
questions.ref: NCMA/CMHA and geotechnical retaining-wall guidance - sliding and overturning stability
questions.n: Rotation about the wall base or toe with pronounced top displacement is characteristic of overturning.

questions.q: What failure mechanism may govern a steel beam whose compression flange is not adequately laterally braced?
questions.ref: AISC guidance on lateral-torsional buckling and slender structural members
questions.n: An unbraced beam can deflect laterally and twist before reaching its full flexural strength.

questions.q: How many structural members form the edges of a tetrahedron?
questions.ref: Daniel L. Schodek et al., Structures - structural systems, space frames, folded plates and diaphragms
questions.n: A tetrahedron has six edges, each corresponding to one member in the basic space-frame unit.

questions.q: A long steel beam reaches instability by lateral movement and twist before the section yields in flexure. What failure mode occurred?
questions.ref: AISC guidance on lateral-torsional buckling and slender structural members
questions.n: Combined lateral displacement and twist under bending is the defining behavior of lateral-torsional buckling.

questions.q: What connection behavior is required at the fixed end of a cantilever steel beam?
questions.ref: AISC Steel Construction Manual - beams, columns, moment connections and structural stability
questions.n: A cantilever must transfer bending moment and shear at its fixed support, so a moment-resisting connection is required.

questions.q: What is the general term for a floor slab supported above ground rather than cast directly on grade?
questions.ref: Francis D.K. Ching, Building Construction Illustrated - structural systems, retaining walls, frames and slabs
questions.n: A suspended slab spans between structural supports and is elevated above the ground or another space.

questions.q: A steel beam projects beyond a column with no support at its outer end. What must the beam-column joint transfer in addition to shear?
questions.ref: AISC Steel Construction Manual - beams, columns, moment connections and structural stability
questions.n: The fixed support of a cantilever develops a significant end moment in addition to shear.

questions.q: A partial floor overlooks the story below and occupies only part of the building footprint. What is it called?
questions.ref: Cyril M. Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction - structural terminology
questions.n: A partial intermediate floor that opens to or overlooks the space below is a mezzanine.

questions.q: What gives a folded-plate roof much of its stiffness?
o: The geometric depth and rigidity created by the folds
questions.ref: Daniel L. Schodek et al., Structures - structural systems, space frames, folded plates and diaphragms
questions.n: The folded geometry creates structural depth and couples adjacent plates, increasing stiffness.

questions.q: Which consideration is fundamental when selecting an initial structural system?
o: A clear load path from applied loads to the foundations
questions.ref: ASCE/SEI 7 - Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and Other Structures
questions.n: A viable structural concept must provide a continuous and understandable path for gravity and lateral forces to reach the foundations.

questions.q: What is interstory drift?
o: The relative horizontal displacement between two adjacent floors
questions.ref: ASCE/SEI 7 - Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and Other Structures
questions.n: Interstory drift measures relative lateral displacement from one level to the next.

questions.q: What is the structural action produced by a twisting moment about a member's longitudinal axis?
questions.ref: Cyril M. Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction - structural terminology
questions.n: Torsion is the twisting action created by torque acting about a member's longitudinal axis.

questions.q: What is a structural diaphragm?
o: A floor or roof plane that transfers in-plane lateral forces to vertical resisting elements
questions.ref: ASCE/SEI 7 - Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and Other Structures
questions.n: Diaphragms distribute lateral loads through the floor/roof plane to shear walls, braced frames, or moment frames.

questions.q: A beam is loaded eccentrically so the applied force tends to twist the beam along its length. What structural action must be checked?
questions.ref: Cyril M. Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction - structural terminology
questions.n: An eccentric load that twists the member produces torsional demand.

questions.q: Which element would not normally be described as a diaphragm by itself?
questions.ref: Daniel L. Schodek et al., Structures - structural systems, space frames, folded plates and diaphragms
questions.n: A diaphragm is a plane system; a single isolated truss is a line element rather than the complete diaphragm plane.

questions.q: What failure mode occurs when the retaining wall translates horizontally along its base?
questions.ref: NCMA/CMHA and geotechnical retaining-wall guidance - sliding and overturning stability
questions.n: Sliding occurs when horizontal driving forces exceed friction and other resisting forces along the base.

questions.q: What is a slender column?
o: A column governed only by concrete color
A short block with no instability risk
A column whose capacity is significantly influenced by buckling
questions.ref: AISC Steel Construction Manual - beams, columns, moment connections and structural stability
questions.n: As column slenderness increases, instability and second-order effects can govern its strength.

questions.q: What is the simplest stable three-dimensional space-frame unit formed by six members?
questions.ref: Daniel L. Schodek et al., Structures - structural systems, space frames, folded plates and diaphragms
questions.n: A tetrahedron has four nodes joined by six edges and is the simplest stable three-dimensional triangulated unit.

questions.q: Why is lateral bracing important for the compression flange of a steel beam?
o: It restrains lateral movement and twist, increasing resistance to lateral-torsional buckling
It acts only as paint support
questions.ref: AISC Steel Construction Manual - beams, columns, moment connections and structural stability
questions.n: Compression-flange restraint reduces the tendency of the beam to buckle laterally and twist under flexure.

questions.q: Why are triangulated space frames structurally efficient?
o: Triangulation provides geometric stability and distributes loads through axial member forces
questions.ref: Daniel L. Schodek et al., Structures - structural systems, space frames, folded plates and diaphragms
questions.n: Triangulation creates stable geometry and allows many members to act primarily in axial tension or compression.
